[TODAY] A dead star's final hours, written in dust. 💥

About 11,000 light-years away lies Cassiopeia A, the cloud left by a massive star whose explosion we first saw about 340 years ago. NASA's Webb telescope has now mapped the dust inside it.

The dust points to a "shell merger": inner layers burning different elements may have mixed, possibly just hours before the blast. Stars like this one spread elements such as the iron in your blood across space.

Reality check: the data support this scenario; it is not a final verdict.

Save this if you like a good cosmic detective story.

[TODAY] 11,000 pounds of science, food and toilet parts. 📦

NASA and Northrop Grumman are targeting Sunday, Nov. 29 to launch a Cygnus XL cargo ship on a Falcon 9 rocket. On Dec. 1, astronauts plan to catch it with the station's robotic arm, Canadarm2.

Inside: food and supplies for the crew, new sleeping-quarter blankets, a replacement toilet hose, plus experiments on muscle loss, cancer spread and growing crops for long missions. A robot will even test welding metal in space.

Reality check: the launch date is a target and can slip. The ship stays until May 2027, then burns up carrying trash.

[TODAY] Why does Venus shine brightest as a crescent? ✨

Venus passed between Earth and the Sun on Oct. 23-24. Now it is racing ahead of us, still close, so through a telescope it looks large. And we see a growing crescent of its sunlit side.

Near and big beats full but far: when Venus is fully lit, it sits on the far side of the Sun and looks tiny. The best mix arrives about five weeks after it passes us, this year on Nov. 29, at magnitude -4.4.

Reality check: the change from one morning to the next is subtle, so any clear dawn this week works.

Save this and look east before sunrise. It won't look this bright at dawn again until July 2028.

[TODAY] A young star is boiling rock into gas. 🔥

About 1,500 light-years away, a massive young star called Orion Source I is so bright it evaporates rock in its disk. With the ALMA telescope, astronomers found titanium oxide gas around such a star for the first time.

Gas has a readable fingerprint; distant rock does not. Heat-loving minerals like this may be the first seeds of rocky planets like Earth.

Reality check: it is one unusual system; comparisons with our solar system have only begun.

[IMAGINE] A dark-matter telescope found a comet by accident. ☄️

What is real: ESA's Euclid telescope maps distant galaxies. In September, new software spotted a streak in its images: an unknown comet, now named C/2026 S1 (Euclid), about 1.3 billion km from Earth on an orbit that takes thousands of years.

ESA is also building Comet Interceptor, planned for late 2028 or early 2029. It is designed to wait in space, 1.5 million km from Earth, for a fresh comet not yet discovered.

Reality check: this comet is not a suitable target, only a test run.

The speculation: what if sky surveys routinely picked targets for spacecraft already waiting?

Comet or interstellar visitor: which should it chase? Tell us below.
